name: Erik Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the keyboard players for a theatre, record accompaniment tracks for singers and teach six piano pupils. I have a music master’s and I earn well, but the best part is watching an actor find the right breath when the orchestra changes tempo with them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the family calendar look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in city planning, and we share pickup for two school-age children around show nights. We have a mortgage and fourteen months of expenses saved, partly because we keep a separate account for touring gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that a faster call sheet, the list of who plays when, would help. I would still expect a paid keyboard player for a live show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have fourteen months saved and current shows and pupils are paying well. There are several other theatres nearby, so a small change to booking software does not threaten our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This season I would keep the keyboard calls, record paid singer tracks and teach six pupils. I already use AI daily to sort rehearsal clips, but I listen to every clip before marking a pupil’s timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm. A plateau changes our paperwork more than our paid playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a show night worth a long journey?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The manager must put the fee and finish time in the call sheet. I would ask for both before accepting an extra out-of-town date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let AI grade a child’s rhythm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I check the beat myself. A clipped phone recording can make a steady pupil sound late.

say: I would welcome **faster call sheets** while keeping live players paid.
I would require **written fees** and finish times for extra dates.
think: Our **fourteen-month reserve** and paid calls protect the mortgage.
Several **nearby theatres** offer similar work if bookings shift.
do: Keep **paid keyboard calls**, singer tracks and six pupils this season.
Request **written fees** and finish times before extra out-of-town dates.
feel: I feel **calm** about secure live work and household income.
S0.quote: A clipped phone recording can make a steady pupil sound late.
fieldNote: His **strong reserve**, paid mix of work and nearby stages make plateau income secure.
His **daily AI clip sorting** is existing use, checked by his own listening.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre keyboard calls, singer tracks and six pupils this season
Request written fee and finish time before extra out-of-town show dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the musicians’ association that generated accompaniment could reduce paid recording days. We should negotiate a minimum fee for human rehearsal and track revisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tracks and revisions are about a third of my own earnings, and a fast generator could take those commissions. The live theatre still needs us now, but its budget might tighten as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would bring a year of recording invoices to the association and ask the theatre for written paid revision hours. In the first year I would attend a paid engineer-led trial of a new tempo checker, then test my own nameless track only with approved in-studio storage; I would compare its beats by ear against the live recording and stop if tempo shifts or the file leaves the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a real slice of my pay disappearing. Fourteen months of savings are time to respond, not a reason to work free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test a student’s singing track?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A child’s voice and name stay in the teaching folder; I can use a track I own without personal details.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take another theatre job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If paid revision or keyboard hours actually fall, I would apply for a posted paid music-director seat only if my master’s qualifies, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and pickup fits; I would keep my current calls until a signed offer. An impressive rehearsal-room title would not compensate for lost recording fees.

I would demand **paid revision hours** in writing.
think: Generated **accompaniment** could remove a third of my earnings.
Some **keyboard calls** may also shrink if the theatre budget tightens.
do: Bring **recording invoices** to the association and request written paid revision hours next month.
Test the **tempo checker** after paid training and approved studio storage on my nameless track; compare by ear, stop errors/leakage.
Apply for a **posted music-director seat** if hours fall, only if qualified, written net after travel replaces losses and pickup fits.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording fees despite our reserve.
S1.quote: Fourteen months of savings are time to respond, not a reason to work free.
fieldNote: He links **collective bargaining** to concrete paid revision and rehearsal hours.
The **new checker trial** requires paid instruction, approved local storage, an owned nameless track and ear comparison.

steps.text: Bring recording invoices to musicians association; request written paid revision hours

Apply for qualified posted director seat after revision/keyboard cuts; written net-after-travel replaces fees, pickup fits
Keep paid keyboard calls until suitable signed offer states hours and pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that AGI by 2028 could supply cheap accompaniment for every audition. I want the live keyboard calendar and rehearsal fee signed before the company changes its plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect accompaniment sales to stop in 2028, and the theatre may cut paid rehearsal calls as generated tracks improve. Playing robots come around 2031, three years later. My recording cheque could vanish before a robot touches a key.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total track invoices and seek a signed paid keyboard calendar. In the first year after 2028, if paid theatre calls fall as well, I would apply for a posted college accompanist job only if my master’s qualifies, written net pay after travel replaces lost track and theatre fees and pickup works; I would keep pupils and paid calls until a signed offer states hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about losing track sales, even with fourteen months saved. If tracks and theatre calls both went, I would be alarmed because that is over half my income. I have caught myself awake calculating that larger loss, but it is not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new keyboard to compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a signed paid booking that covers its cost after the players are paid. I would keep nine months of household expenses untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the college job is just mentioned in a hallway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep playing and teaching. A real posted vacancy with written hours comes before an application.

I would apply for a **posted college role** after actual paid-call cuts.
think: **Track sales** likely end in 2028 before 2031 playing robots.

do: Count **track invoices** and request a signed paid keyboard calendar now.
Apply for **posted accompanist work** after 2028 call cuts if qualified, written net after travel replaces losses and pickup fits.
Keep **pupils and paid calls** until a suitable signed offer states hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected track losses; losing theatre calls too would alarm me.
S2.quote: My recording cheque could vanish before a robot touches a key.
fieldNote: His **2028 recording loss** precedes physical playing robots around 2031.
A **college move** requires actual paid call loss, qualified posted job, written net replacement, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Count track invoices and request signed paid theatre keyboard calendar now
Apply for qualified posted college accompanist after 2028 call cuts; replacement written net-after-travel pay, pickup
Keep six pupils and paid calls until suitable signed offer states hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the cast that five years until AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn how to make live sound accessible. A recorded track is not the only way a listener can follow a show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Track fees may disappear by 2031 and keyboard robots could appear around 2034. A paid accessibility role could broaden my work, but the course has to lead to a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would take a six-month audio-access course, training to prepare sound for people with hearing differences, only if the theatre funds it, pays the study hours and pickup costs my partner no shifts. In the first year after 2031, if paid track or keyboard hours fall, I would apply for a posted theatre audio-access job only if the certificate qualifies me, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and pickup fits; I would keep paid calls and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the track income, though a funded route gives me time to move. I would not spend our nine-month floor on a course with no paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you mix a live show alone after the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The theatre sound lead would supervise the first assisted show. I would not run a crowded performance alone until the equipment and access checks are signed off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is funded but unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on paid keyboard calls and ask for a paid intake. Free tuition does not replace a wage while I study.

I would pursue a **posted audio-access role** if track or keyboard hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that a decade until AGI by 2036 lets us build paid human music jobs with clear contracts. The musicians’ association should count every lost track fee, not just the final performance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Track sales may stop by 2036 and playing robots may threaten keyboard chairs around 2039. We have time and several nearby employers, but I do not want the mortgage to depend on a single theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this year I would save ten percent of every extra paid accompaniment licence after mortgage, food and pupil travel, aiming for eighteen months while leaving nine untouched. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid calls and pupils and apply for a posted conservatory keyboard lead only if my master’s qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost track and stage fees and pickup fits; I would leave only when a signed offer states hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about a distant change, with a long reserve and local options. I would still want the new post in writing before I moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if licence sales end before the goal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save only spare paid lesson fees after household bills. I would protect nine months of expenses rather than pay for speculative auditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a prestigious but unpaid lead title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The written net fee after travel has to beat the lost work. A conservatory keyboard-lead title is decoration without paid work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because track sales and paid rehearsal calls could fall together. Signed theatre calls, a posted qualified college role and pickup that works would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid for the first rehearsal after a software change. A new score is not a free afternoon for the players.

headlineQuote: A new score is not a free afternoon for the players.
portrait: At **43**, Erik leads theatre keyboard players with a music master’s, two children, a mortgage and fourteen months saved.
His higher **musician pay** comes from live calls, accompaniment licences and six pupils.
He uses **AI daily** but tests a new tempo checker only after paid training, approved storage and listening checks.
A **funded audio-access course** needs paid hours and pickup without lost partner shifts before a posted qualified job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove track sales and paid rehearsal calls together.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed theatre calls**, a qualified posted college role with written net pay and workable pickup would help Erik.
